claim: The war was fought over slavery; its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism.
quote: The war was fought over slavery. Its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism.
lineage: the settlement reorganized the labor topology

claim: Two axes, moving separately: the juridical scope of the claim on the worker, and the grain at which productive activity is measured.
quote: Two quantities move, and they move separately. The first is the juridical scope of the claim on the worker: the person and the lifetime, or labor-power for a bounded interval. The second is the grain at which productive activity is measured: life, year, day, hand, task, motion, second.
lineage: two axes: juridical scope and measurement grain

claim: Emancipation is a discontinuity in the scope axis; Taylor and Ford a change in the grain; the claim narrows as measurement becomes finer.
quote: Emancipation is a discontinuity in the first. Taylor and Ford are a change in the second. The legal claim narrows while the measurement of the activity becomes finer.
lineage: two axes: juridical scope and measurement grain

claim: The field holds that slavery and its expansion caused secession and the war.
quote: The field holds that slavery and its expansion caused secession and the war.

claim: Mississippi's 1861 declaration identifies its position with slavery.
quote: Mississippi's declaration of 1861 opens its case: "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery-- the greatest material interest of the world."

claim: Marx, October 1861: the Morrill tariff passed because secession had taken place, and not the reverse.
quote: Marx said so in October 1861, answering the London papers that had discovered the tariff as the cause. He noted that the Morrill tariff passed Congress "only in 1861, after the rebellion had already broken out", and concluded: "Secession, therefore, did not take place because the Morrill tariff had gone through Congress, but, at most, the Morrill tariff went through Congress because secession had taken place."

claim: Marx: the whole movement was based on the slave question.
quote: His own verdict: "The whole movement was and is based, as one sees, on the slave question."

claim: Ransom reports Gunderson: in the eleven Confederate states slaves were 38 percent of the population and contributed 23 percent of whites' income.
quote: He reports Gunderson's estimate that for all eleven Confederate states "slaves represented 38 percent of the population and contributed 23 percent of whites' income".

claim: The stake was slavery itself: its value as property and its need for territory.
quote: The stake was slavery itself: its value as property and its need for territory.

claim: The Beard-Hacker thesis was the most widely accepted interpretation of the war's economic impact by the Second World War.
quote: By the Second World War the "Beard-Hacker Thesis" "had become the most widely accepted interpretation of the economic impact of the Civil War", and it was still "the prevailing view as late as 1960".

claim: As an account of causes the Beard-Hacker thesis was abandoned after about 1950.
quote: As an account of causes it was abandoned after about 1950.

claim: As an account of consequences, quantitative economic history cut the thesis down (Cochran 1961; Engerman).
quote: As an account of consequences it was cut down by quantitative economic history: Thomas Cochran argued in 1961 that the war retarded industrial growth, and Stanley Engerman challenged the claim that the 1862 Republican program accelerated it.

claim: The research behind the paper found no post-2000 scholarship arguing the North went to war for cheap wage labor.
quote: The research behind this paper found no post-2000 scholarship that argues the North went to war to obtain cheap wage labor for its industry.
lineage: the North did not fight for labor

claim: The field's political economy of the war is a collision of two labor systems (Oakes: slaves owned as property, Northern laborers self-owned).
quote: The field's political economy of the war is a collision of two labor systems. James Oakes states the axis in its plainest form: "At the heart of that difference was the fact that slaves were owned as property whereas in the North, laborers owned themselves".

claim: Emancipation abolished property in persons; the Thirteenth Amendment was passed 31 January and ratified 6 December 1865, with its exception for punishment for crime.
quote: Emancipation abolished property in persons. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress on 31 January 1865 and ratified on 6 December 1865, reads: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction."
lineage: the Thirteenth Amendment and its exception

claim: The paper accepts the conventional reading; its object is the measurement of the laboring body before and after the abolition of property in it.
quote: This paper accepts all of 0.1–0.7. Its object is what the conventional reading leaves in the background: the measurement of the laboring body before and after the abolition of property in it.

claim: The war changed what capital could own; the techniques converting human capacity into a number survived it and changed object.
quote: The war changed what capital could own. The techniques that converted human capacity into a number survived it and changed object.
lineage: the settlement reorganized the labor topology

claim: The Savannah sale of 1859: Guy sold at $1,280, Andrew, his counterpart save a lost right eye, at $1,040; the reporter prices the eye at $240.
quote: "Guy, chattel No. 419, 'a prime young man,' sold for $1,280, being without blemish; his age was twenty years, and he was altogether a fine article. His next-door neighbor, Andrew, chattel No. 420, was his very counterpart in all marketable points, in size, age, skill, and everything save that he had lost his right eye. Andrew sold for only $1,040, from which we argue that the market value of the right eye in the Southern country is $240."

claim: The $240 arithmetic is the reporter's, sardonic, and exact because the market had made the two men comparable.
quote: The arithmetic is the reporter's, and sardonic ("from which we argue"). It is exact because the market had already made the two men comparable "in all marketable points".

claim: Rosenthal: slaveholders developed the 'prime field hand' as an equivalence unit, with expected production per day.
quote: Rosenthal: "Slaveholders also developed an equivalence unit called 'the prime field hand.' They assigned certain capabilities to the prime hand, such as expected production per day. Workers were measured against this standard and given values such as 'half hand' and 'quarter hand.'"
lineage: the hand: a verb-measure on a noun

claim: The hand grades a whole person's daily output as a fraction of an adult male standard, a verb-measure attached to a noun; the inference is the paper's.
quote: It grades a whole person's daily output as a fraction of an adult male standard: a verb-measure attached to a noun.
lineage: the hand: a verb-measure on a noun

claim: Under slavery American capitalism developed techniques for measuring, comparing and monetizing human capacity, which worked because the worker was owned.
quote: The record supports this much: American capitalism developed, under slavery, techniques for measuring, comparing and monetizing human capacity, and those techniques worked because the worker was owned.
lineage: the hand: a verb-measure on a noun

claim: No source consulted documents a line from plantation records to Taylor or Ford; the argument needs none.
quote: No source consulted for this paper documents a line from plantation records to Taylor or Ford, and the argument needs none.

claim: The grain of measurement is its own axis; what emancipation changed was the scope of the claim.
quote: The grain of measurement is therefore its own axis, independent of the scope of the claim: slavery could already contract its unit to the years it took to use a person up, to the day's quota and to the fraction of a hand. What emancipation changed was the scope of the claim.
lineage: two axes: juridical scope and measurement grain

claim: Hammond, 1858: slaves 'hired for life', the North's hirelings 'hired by the day'.
quote: James Henry Hammond, in the Senate, 4 March 1858: "The senator from New York said yesterday that the whole world had abolished slavery. Aye, the name, but not the thing… for the man who lives by daily labor, and scarcely lives at that, and who has to put out his labor in the market, and take the best he can get for it; in short, your whole hireling class of manual laborers and 'operatives,' as you call them, are essentially slaves. The difference between us is, that our slaves are hired for life and well compensated… Yours are hired by the day, not cared for, and scantily compensated…

claim: Lincoln at Milwaukee, 1859, reports the mud-sill reasoning in two verbs, hire and buy, and his own side holds both assumptions false.
quote: Lincoln answered the mud-sill theory at Milwaukee on 30 September 1859. He reported its reasoning in two verbs. Its adherents assume "that labor is available only in connection with capital", and then "proceed to consider whether it is best that capital shall hire laborers, and thus induce them to work by their own consent; or buy them, and drive them to it without their consent."

claim: Lincoln's clause moralizing the permanent wage-earner as dependent is read as the seed of postwar discipline.
quote: The person who stays on the wage is moralized as dependent. That clause is the seed of the postwar discipline in §4.

claim: On these texts slavery sold the person and wage labor sold capacity for an interval; the difference is legal title to the person.
quote: On these texts slavery sold the person, the noun, and wage labor sold capacity for an interval, the verb. The noun owned and the verb contracted are different relations, and the difference is legal title to the person.

claim: Postwar wage earners argued that in selling their labor they were no more self-owning than slaves (Stanley).
quote: Amy Dru Stanley reports their argument that "in selling their labor they were no more self-owning than slaves".

claim: Marx, 7 November 1861: the struggle is between two social systems, slavery and free labour.
quote: "The present struggle between the South and North is, therefore, nothing but a struggle between two social systems, the system of slavery and the system of free labour.

claim: Marx reads the war as a contest over where the line of unfree labor would run across the continent and the races of labor.
quote: Marx reads the war as a contest over where the line of unfree labor would run across the continent and across the races of labor.

claim: Marx, Capital ch. 10: the first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation.
quote: The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation, that ran with the seven-leagued boots of the locomotive from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from New England to California."
lineage: the first fruit: the eight hours

claim: The Baltimore General Congress of Labour, 16 August 1866, called for an eight-hour law.
quote: The General Congress of Labour at Baltimore, 16 August 1866: "The first and great necessity of the present, to free the labour of this country from capitalistic slavery, is the passing of a law by which eight hours shall be the normal working-day in all States of the American Union."
lineage: the first fruit: the eight hours

claim: Once the noun could no longer be sold, the contested object became the length of the day.
quote: The first fruit Marx names is a struggle over the measure of the verb. Once the noun could no longer be sold, the contested object became the length of the day: the interval.
lineage: the first fruit: the eight hours

claim: Du Bois: the black worker won the war by a general strike transferring his labor to the Northern invader.
quote: "How the Civil War meant emancipation and how the black worker won the war by a general strike which transferred his labor from the Confederate planter to the Northern invader, in whose army lines workers began to be organized as a new labor force."

claim: The general strike is read as the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner; the workers reorganized the topology by moving.
quote: The general strike is the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner. The workers reorganized the topology themselves, by moving.

claim: Du Bois: the slave went free, stood a brief moment in the sun, then moved back toward slavery.
quote: "The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery."
lineage: the settlement closed toward contract and debt

claim: Du Bois's public and psychological wage compensated white laborers in part.
quote: "It must be remembered that the white group of laborers, while they received a low wage, were compensated in part by a sort of public and psychological wage.

claim: Du Bois is a source for the general strike and the settlement, a weaker one for Northern motive.
quote: Du Bois is a source for the general strike and the settlement. He is a weaker source for Northern motive.

claim: Oakes credits Du Bois with seeing emancipation as a capitalist revolution, its replacement a system based on wage labor, and faults his treatment of the North.
quote: Oakes credits him with understanding "that emancipation was a capitalist revolution, that the truly revolutionary character of the Civil War lay in the overthrow of slavery and its replacement by a new system based on wage labor", and faults his treatment of the North, which "too often collapsed into crude economic determinism".
lineage: the settlement reorganized the labor topology

claim: The Act to Encourage Immigration, 4 July 1864, is called the most direct federal instrument of labor supply in the war years.
quote: The Act to Encourage Immigration, 4 July 1864, is the most direct federal instrument of labor supply in the war years.

claim: Sec. 2 of the 1864 Act made emigrants' pledges of up to twelve months' wages to repay emigration valid in law.
quote: whereby emigrants shall pledge the wages of their labor for a term not exceeding twelve months to repay the expenses of their emigration, shall be held to be valid in law

claim: Pledged wages are read as the verb mortgaged in advance, the debt following the worker onto homestead land.
quote: Wages for up to twelve months are pledged before the work exists: the verb mortgaged in advance. The debt follows the worker onto the land the Homestead Law promised, the material of Lincoln's ladder.

claim: The statute disclaims 'the relation of Slavery or servitude', seven months before Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment.
quote: And the statute disclaims "the relation of Slavery or servitude", seven months before Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment.

claim: The UT Immigration History project records that Congress repealed the law in 1868 in the face of labor protests.
quote: records that "In the face of vociferous protests by labor organizations, Congress repealed this law in 1868."
